items.actClause:
AN ACT to amend the education law, in relation to the compulsory age for full
time instruction and certain related exceptions
items.memo:
BILL NUMBER: S4037

SPONSOR: SKOUFIS
 
TITLE OF BILL:

An act to amend the education law, in relation to the compulsory age for
full time instruction and certain related exceptions

 
PURPOSE:

This bill lowers the compulsory age of full-time school attendance to
five years of age, from the current age of six. It requires that all
children between the ages of five to sixteen years of age attend school
full-time.

 
SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS:

Section 1: Amends subdivision 11 of section 2 of the education law,
which defines the term "child of compulsory school age."

Section 2: Amends subdivision 1, paragraph c of subdivision 2, and
subdivision 3 of section 3205 of the education law, which states that
children aged five to sixteen in all school districts must attend school
full-time. Section 2 also states that a parent may elect not to enroll
their child in school in the school year the child is five years old. In
such case, the parent shall submit a written notice to the school
district superintendent in which the child resides by no later than the
first day of April.

Section 3: Sets Effective Date.

 
JUSTIFICATION:

Experts agree that early childhood education plays a critical role in
later school success and the crucial developmental period of brain
growth. Kindergarten, in particular, helps to lay the foundation for all
there is to come by promoting everything from basic academic skills like
reading-readiness and early math to honing crucial social talents such
as patience, perseverance, determination, and manners.  Some research
revealed longitudinal benefits by showing that children who learned more
in kindergarten were less likely to be single parents, went to college
in higher numbers, and earned higher incomes.

While New York has worked to offer every-four year old a seat in the
Universal Pre-K program, kindergarten in New York is not mandatory,
largely partly due to the current education law, which sets the compul-
sory age for full-time school attendance at six. As a result, many
school districts complain of chronic absenteeism - where more than 31
days of school are missed -among their five-year-old students. Some
parents perceive early education, particularly in kindergarten, as unim-
portant. At the same time, contrary research has shown that chronic
absence in kindergarten is associated with lower academic performance in
the first grade. By lowering the mandatory attendance age to five years,
we give children the early tools they need to succeed. This bill is
modeled after provisions from legislation previously advanced by the
State Education Department.

FISCAL IMPLICATIONS:

To be determined.

 
EFFECTIVE DATE:
This act shall take effect on the first of July next succeeding the date
on which it shall have become a law.

AN ACT to amend the education law, in relation to the compulsory age for full
time instruction and certain related exceptions; and requires kindergarten in

C.memo:
BILL NUMBER: S4037C

SPONSOR: SKOUFIS
 
TITLE OF BILL:

An act to amend the education law, in relation to the compulsory age for
full time instruction and certain related exceptions; and requires
kindergarten in certain school districts

 
PURPOSE:

The bill lowers the compulsory age of full-time school attendance to
five years of age, from the current age of six. It requires that all
children between the ages of five to sixteen years of age attend school
full-time. It further requires that the board of education for a school
district maintains a kindergarten for residents between the ages of four
and six at no cost to the attendee.

 
SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS:

Section 1: Amends subdivision 11 of section 2 of the education law,
which defines the term "child of compulsory school age."

Section 2: Amends subdivision 1, paragraph c of subdivision 2, and
subdivision 3 of section 3205 of the education law, which states that
children in all school districts must attend school full-time.

Section 2 also states that a minor who will become five years of age in
any school year and whose parent elects not to enroll their child in
school or in home instruction in such school year shall not be required
to attend upon full time instruction until the first day of session in
September of the following school year.

Section 3: Amends subdivision 1 of section 4105 of the education law to
make similar changes related to Native American schools.

Section 4: Amends section 4106 of the education law to make similar
changes related to Native American schools.

Section 5: Amends section 4108 of the education law to make similar
changes related to Native American schools.

Section 6: Amends section 4109 of the education law to make similar
changes related to Native American schools.

Section 7: Amends section 4111 of the education law to make similar
changes related to Native American schools.

Section 8: Amends subdivision 1 of section 1712 of the education law to
require the board of education of each union free school district to
maintain free kindergartens for resident children between the ages of
four and six.

Section 9: Amends subdivision 1 of section 2514 of the education law
require the board of education of each city school district of a city
with less than 125,000 inhabitants to maintain free kindergartens for
resident children between the ages of four and six.


Section 10: amends subdivision 1 of section 2555 of the education law to
require the board of education of each school district of a city with
more than 125,000 inhabitants to maintain free kindergartens for resi-
dent children between the ages of four and six.

Section 11: Sets Effective Date.

Experts agree that early childhood education plays a critical role in

sory age for full-time school attendance at six. As a result, many
school districts complain of chronic absenteeism, where more than 10% of
